title: Words From a Single Key Row
statement:
A QWERTY keyboard has three rows of letter keys:

  • top: qwertyuiop
  • middle: asdfghjkl
  • bottom: zxcvbnm

You get a list of words made of upper- and lowercase letters. Return the words whose letters all lie on one row, in their original order. Case does not matter: "Q" is on the top row like "q". Return each kept word exactly as written.

examples.why: "Mix" needs the bottom row for m and x but the top row for i.
Both z keys are on the bottom row. In "cab", c and b are on the bottom row but a is in the middle: checking only the first letter's row is not enough.
o is on the top row and k in the middle; h is in the middle and i on top. An empty list is a valid answer.

hints: For every letter you need to know its row. How can you look that up in O(1)?
Build a map from each lowercase letter to its row number, once.
A word qualifies when every letter, lowercased, has the same row as its first letter.

explain.intuition:
Each letter belongs to exactly one row, so turn the keyboard into a lookup table: letter → row. Then a word passes when all its letters map to the same row. Lowercase each letter before the lookup so that case does not matter, but push the original word into the answer.

It is the same pattern as validating a form field against an allowed character set: build the set once, then check each character in O(1).
steps: Build row: for each of the three row strings, map each of its letters to that row's index.
Keep the word if every letter c has row[lowercase(c)] === r.
Return the kept words in input order.
pitfalls: Forgetting to lowercase before the lookup, so capital letters map to no row.
Pushing the lowercased word into the answer instead of the original.
Checking only whether each letter is on some row (they all are) instead of on the same row.

complexity.space: O(1) for the table, plus the output

solutions.title: Test each row as a set
solutions.idea: For each word, try the three rows and check whether the row contains every letter of the lowercased word.

solutions.title: Letter-to-row table
solutions.idea: Map every letter to its row once. A word qualifies when all its letters share the row of its first letter.

followups: Support any keyboard layout given as a list of row strings. What changes?
Return words that need at most two rows. How would you count rows per word?
